editorial.summary: A page-by-page reading of Kevin Eastman's Raphael micro-series becomes David Choe's uncensored account of formative comics, childhood drawing, vigilante fantasy, creator ownership, Japanese fan-comics encounters and the bond between two outsiders. The record preserves explicit, violent, sexual, racial, religious and queer speech while distinguishing printed-page evidence, Choe's memories, host interpretation, rumor and current fact.

quality.assessment: Complete human read and full-source correction/context pass. Dense proper-name damage is repaired where defensible; unresolved audio remains unresolved. Automatic captions contain no publisher speaker prefixes.

editorial.speaker_policy: The public panel is Jim Rugg, Ed Piskor and David Choe, but participant identity does not prove individual lines. Publish no named turns until held-out acoustic and video validation passes.

connections.relationship: A solitary childhood medium becomes a social and intimate adult experience.
Music, profanity, sex, color and underground drawing arrive together in one remembered backpack.
Raphael and Casey provide Choe an analogy for his working friendship with Harry Kim.
The comic's editorial pages preserve the transition from independent hit to licensed franchise.
Childhood access and remembered prices become a story about how objects acquire cultural and financial value.
The hosts use Eastman and Laird to argue for retaining energy and rights in one's own work.
Line, tone, paper, lettering and printing shape the experience independently of plot.
Childhood fantasy is placed beside 1980s screen violence and real urban fear without making influence causal.
Raphael becomes the limit on Casey's violence rather than merely another violent hero.
A family restriction on D&D redirects Choe toward TMNT role-playing and drawing.
Choe contrasts schoolyard legend with what the original comic actually contains.
Environmental detail and controlled reveals make a street fight legible as atmosphere and sequence.
A remembered web listing illustrates how quickly unverified sale lore attaches to major original art.
The panel's explicit jokes are preserved as viewer interpretation rather than page-level fact.
Childhood copies and inventions document practice, influence and family material support.
Toy and fictional weapon fascination later crosses into actual possession and use claims.
Raphael and Casey bond because each recognizes another misfit rather than because conflict disappears.
A personal store visit opens a discussion of dōjinshi and yaoi, but cannot stand for a whole culture.
Backup stories and color reprints show how later editions reshape a single issue.
Bisley, Bodē, graffiti books and TMNT are treated as a mutually reinforcing visual lineage.
Choe names both the sustaining and limiting effects of retaining childhood obsessions.
Comics' lower capital threshold becomes the basis for a plea to make stories too particular for Hollywood.

editorial.description: A page-by-page reading of Kevin Eastman's Raphael micro-series becomes David Choe's uncensored account of formative comics, childhood drawing, vigilante fantasy, creator ownership, Japanese fan-comics encounters and the bond between two outsiders.
